claims.text: The wear performance of HEA protective coatings is primarily governed by rapid formation and dynamic stabilization of a protective tribo-oxide layer during wear.
Increased oxygen availability enhances formation and stabilization of the protective tribo-oxide layer.
The initial HEA coating has a multiphase microstructure.
The initial HEA coating has an inherent tendency to oxidize.
The initial coating does not have a pre-formed protective oxide layer.
Wear tests should compare atmospheres ranging from inert conditions below 1% O2 to ambient air at approximately 21% O2 while temperature, load, and sliding speed are held constant.
During wear, a thin, continuous, self-adaptive tribochemical oxide layer forms on the HEA coating surface.
Increasing oxygen partial pressure accelerates oxidation kinetics at the sliding contact interface.
Accelerated interfacial oxidation produces a continuous protective oxide film more rapidly.
The tribo-oxide film continuously re-passivates the coating surface during sliding.
Continuous re-passivation by the tribo-oxide film reduces abrasive wear and plastic deformation.
Higher-oxygen conditions will produce lower HEA-coating wear rates than inert conditions.
Higher-oxygen conditions will produce a more continuous and adherent tribo-oxide layer than inert conditions.
Very low oxygen availability results in little oxide formation and higher wear rates.
The proposed relationship should hold near 25°C over loads and sliding speeds for which oxide regeneration can compete with mechanical removal.
The proposed relationship may fail when mechanical disruption of the oxide overwhelmingly exceeds its regeneration rate.
A failure of increased oxygen to cause both a statistically significant wear-rate reduction and formation of a continuous protective tribo-oxide layer would falsify the hypothesis.
